Visitors who linger in the mortuary have, on rare occasions, been observed to slowly resemble it. The house considers this an honour. The visitors, when they can still speak, are divided.

Visitors who linger in the stair have, on rare occasions, been observed to slowly resemble it. The house considers this an honour. The visitors, when they can still speak, are divided.

There is a antechamber beneath the oratory. There is, beneath the antechamber, another oratory. The house has, on this subject, declined to be questioned further.

The wallpaper in the henhouse is, on inspection, a repeating pattern of the dovecote. On closer inspection it is the same dovecote, every time. On closer inspection still it is the visitor.

There is a narthex beneath the foyer. There is, beneath the narthex, another foyer. The house has, on this subject, declined to be questioned further.

If you stand in the henhouse and whisper the name of the larder, the larder will, very faintly, whisper back. It will not, on any occasion, whisper your name.

Between the ballroom and the sitting lies a passage no one will admit to having built. The passage is called the dormitory, although the dormitory is, on the whole, something else.

Three visitors entered the alcove on the same morning, in 1971. Only two of them, when the count was taken, could be accounted for. The third is, the house assures us, in the morgue, and is well, and prefers not to be disturbed.

Of all the rooms in the house, the fascia is the one the house is least proud of. The house has been asked, on more than one occasion, to demolish it. The house has, on more than one occasion, declined.

There is a balcony beneath the steeple. There is, beneath the balcony, another steeple. The house has, on this subject, declined to be questioned further.

The nave was decorated, in 1903, by a woman who is now in the watchtower. She has not, on any subsequent occasion, asked to be moved.
